result:
There is a strange, quiet moment that happens just after you close a book but before you stand up. The story is finished, but you are still inside it. The room around you hasn't quite come back into focus yet. The air conditioner hums in a different century than the one you were just living in. That threshold — between worlds — is where I want to live for a while, if you'll sit with me.

I want to talk about attention. Not in the productivity-hack, life-optimization sense. I mean attention as a form of love. Attention as a form of time travel.

When I was nine, I kept a box under my bed. It wasn't a treasure chest in the pirate sense. It was a shoebox, and inside it were things that had completely stopped being what they were supposed to be: a smooth river stone with a white quartz vein running through it like lightning, a blue jay feather, a ticket stub from a train I barely remembered riding, a plastic army man with his rifle melted into a sort of abstract cane, a key that didn't open anything anyone could identify. My mother kept asking me to throw it away. "It's just junk," she would say, not unkindly.

But to me, none of it was junk. Each object had been *chosen*. That act of choosing had transformed it. Psychologists call this the "endowment effect" now. Anthropologists might call it ritual. I just called it my box. The feather wasn't a feather. It was *the day* I found the feather, when my grandfather taught me how to be still enough that the squirrels in the park would forget I was a predator and come close.

We grow up and we learn to curate more acceptable boxes. Playlists, photo rolls, carefully arranged bookshelves that say something about who we wish we were. But the impulse is the same. We are trying to build a little altar to the fact that we were *here*, and that *here* was briefly beautiful.

And that is attention. Attention is what turns a stone into a relic.

We live in a time that is very confused about attention. Our economy runs on it. Companies worth more than nations fight to harvest it, to slice it into thinner and thinner increments, to sell predictions about where it will flicker next. We talk about "paying attention" as if attention were a currency, which now, literally, it is. We talk about having an "attention span" as if it were a muscle that has atrophied because we didn't do enough attention push-ups.

But attention is older and stranger than that. The word itself comes from the Latin *attendere*, which means "to stretch toward." Think about that image. Not to seize, not to consume, not to process. To stretch toward. Attention is an act of reaching. It is the opposite of grasping. It is your mind leaning in the direction of something, like a plant leaning toward light.

Simone Weil, the French philosopher and mystic, wrote that "Attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer." She didn't mean prayer as reciting requests. She meant prayer as a complete, generous, un-selfing orientation toward reality as it actually is. To really attend to something — a person, a tree, a problem in mathematics, a line of music — is to temporarily suspend your own agenda long enough to let it speak on its own terms.

We rarely do that. It's terrifying to do that.

Because to really attend to the world is to realize how much of it you have missed. I spent thirty years walking past a particular species of tree in my neighborhood every day before someone told me its name was a Ginkgo, a living fossil, essentially unchanged for 200 million years. Dinosaurs ate its leaves. Its fan-shaped leaves turn a shocking, almost neon yellow in the fall, all at once. For one week a year, my block is littered with yellow fans from the Jurassic. I had seen it as "background tree." I had scrolled past it in real life.

How many background trees are in your life right now? How many people?

There is a wonderful term from biology: *umwelt*. Coined by Jakob von Uexküll, it refers to the specific sensory world of an organism. The umwelt of a tick is temperature, butyric acid, and touch. The umwelt of a human is very different. The umwelt of a bat, built from echolocation, is almost impossible for us to imagine. We all live on the same planet, but we do not live in the same world.

The melancholy and the miracle is that even between two humans, the umwelten do not quite overlap. My blue is not your blue. My childhood kitchen smells nothing like yours. When we try to describe grief or falling in love, we are like travelers trying to describe a color the other person has never seen. We use metaphors as crutches: "It felt like falling." "It felt like drowning." We triangulate.

Art is the technology we invented for smuggling our umwelt into someone else's head. A novel is a machine for borrowing another nervous system for a few hours. A song is a way of saying, "This is what my sadness sounded like at 3 p.m. on a Tuesday in 2014, does it sound like yours at all?" And sometimes — miraculously — it does. Someone in Seoul listens to a blues song recorded in Mississippi in 1937 and says *yes, that's it exactly.*

That's why we need stories that aren't "content." Content is something you consume and replace. A story is something you enter and are changed by. Content wants your eyeballs. A story wants your stretched-towardness.

I think we are hungry for slowness without knowing how to ask for it. We go on vacations where we promise ourselves we will "unplug" and then we feel anxious when we do. We buy journals we don't write in. We download meditation apps that gamify breathing, which is a little like putting a speedometer on a nap.

Slowness is not laziness. Slowness is precision. Anybody can skim. It takes expertise and care to read closely. A great birdwatcher is not someone who sees more birds; it's someone who sees *one bird* more completely. They notice the way a warbler flicks its tail, the difference between a song and a call, the habitat it prefers. Their world becomes higher resolution.

We can train our resolution. Not through discipline in the punitive sense, but through invitation. Try this, if you like, sometime today: pick one small thing and give it ninety seconds of uninterrupted, stretched-toward attention. Not to photograph it. Not to identify it. Just to notice it.

It could be your own hand. Look at it as if you have never seen one before. The constellations of lines on the palm, the topography of knuckles, the way the fingernails grow in imperfect ovals. Your hand is the tool that has touched every person you have ever loved. It is an archive of your work, your nervous habits, your injuries.

Or pick a cup of tea. Feel the weight of it. Watch the steam make its brief, chaotic calligraphy against the air and vanish. That steam is the cup exhaling. In a few minutes, the liquid will be cooler and the world will have rearranged itself by a fraction of a degree.

Ninety seconds feels absurdly long at first. The mind will try to check out. It will offer you a to-do list, a cringe memory from 2012, a sudden urge to check the news. That isn't failure. That's just the mind doing its restless monkey dance. Gently, without scolding it, bring the stretched-towardness back.

What you will find is that ninety seconds is enough for the thing to start giving something back. It stops being "a hand" or "a cup" and becomes particular. It becomes *this* hand, *this* cup, on *this* afternoon that will never happen again.

Time, I think, is not what we think it is. We picture it as a line, an arrow, a river flowing past. But our lived experience of time doesn't feel like that at all. Sometimes an hour feels like three days — waiting for medical results, a long night when you cannot sleep. Sometimes a whole summer disappears in the rearview mirror and you think, where did it go?

Einstein proved that time is relative to gravity and velocity, but every child knows time is relative to attention and love. The most boring meeting of your life and the first hour with someone you adore contain the same sixty minutes by the clock, but they are not the same amount of time. Not even close.

Maybe time isn't a river we are floating down. Maybe time is something we *make* with our attention. When we are distracted and everywhere, we make thin, papery time that tears easily and leaves no trace. When we are fully present, we make thick, dense time, time with weight and texture. Years later, you can still sink into it.

That's why childhood summers feel so long. Children are natural contemplatives. They haven't yet learned to divide their attention into fifty streams. When a child plays, they play with their whole being. When they look at a beetle, the rest of the universe politely waits.

We can return to that, not by becoming childlike in a naive way, but by becoming childlike in an attentive way.

There's a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*, often translated as "the pathos of things" or "the bittersweetness of impermanence." It's the gentle sadness you feel when you see cherry blossoms falling. Not because you wish they would stay, but precisely because they don't. Their beauty is inseparable from their brevity. In fact, their brevity is what sharpens the beauty to a point fine enough to pierce you.

Western culture tends to fight impermanence. We build wrinkle creams and hard drives and monuments and legacies, all beautiful attempts to say "stay." Japanese aesthetics often do the opposite. They build a temple of wood knowing it will burn and be rebuilt. They arrange flowers knowing they will wilt. They make a tea bowl that is deliberately imperfect, cracked and mended with gold — *kintsugi* — to honor the history of breakage rather than hide it.

What if our anxiety is not that things are impermanent, but that we are only half-present while they are here? The cherry blossom doesn't grieve its own falling. We grieve that we were looking at our phones while it fell.

So here's my small, unoriginal, earnest wish for you, whoever you are, reading this in whatever year, on whatever device, in whatever mood you brought to this page:

May you have at least one moment today where you are completely where you are.

May you notice one small wonder without needing to monetize it or share it or turn it into a lesson. Like the way late afternoon light makes dust visible, like galaxies. Like the way a dog sighs when it finally lies down. Like the particular blue of the sky just after the sun has gone but before the stars have the confidence to appear.

May you stretch toward something — a person, a problem, a tree, your own breath — with a little more generosity than yesterday.

And may you keep a shoebox, literal or invisible, for the world as it actually is: strange, cracked, luminous, ordinary, brief, and — if we are paying attention — absolutely full of lightning in the stone.

You won't remember every word of what you read here, and you don't need to. I won't remember writing it quite the same way tomorrow. But maybe, for a minute, we shared a little umwelt. Maybe time got a little thicker while we were together.

If you close this now and look up, the room will come back into focus. The hum will resolve itself into whatever it always was. And somewhere, just outside your window or just inside your mind, a small yellow fan from the Jurassic will be waiting patiently to be seen for the first time.

Thanks for stretching toward this for a while.
